source.title: A Halloween event advertised a $500 costume contest that didn't exist, so I organized a small rebellion that succeeded.
source.text:
I take Halloween more seriously than any reasonable adult should, so this year I went as Zoltar and spent an embarrassing amount of time and money on props, 100 custom-printed, wildly inappropriate fortunes, and even a website. I’m also an unemployed marketing director, so naturally I worked in a little self-promotion. 

The job market has apparently driven me to networking from inside a fortune-telling machine.

The motivation for this absurd undertaking was a Halloween event advertising a $500 cash prize for best costume. Unfortunately, when I arrived, the contest appeared to exist exclusively in their marketing materials. I spoke with over 10 employees, including the GM, and nobody knew anything about it.  
I was pissed, but fortunately Zoltar was a hit, so I started telling everyone who approached me about this grave injustice and encouraging them to comment “JUSTICE FOR ZOLTAR” on the promoter’s Instagram.

Apparently, drunk twenty-somethings are remarkably easy to radicalize, because they actually flooded the comments demanding compensation for a fictional fortune teller.

The next day, the promoters called me, declared me the undisputed winner, sent me $500, and offered me VIP access to a future event.

I’ve now won Halloween two years in a row, although this year apparently required a small populist uprising.  
I’ve worked in marketing for years, and it’s mildly concerning that one of my more successful campaigns involved mobilizing drunk strangers on behalf of a man in a box.

[Pic for full effect.](https://imgur.com/gallery/H01aApm#LoecNX1)

notes: Drinking removed (party crowd). The marketing-job setup in scene 1 pays off in the 'man in a box' button.
